unit.title: Perform basic welding using manual metal arc welding process (MMAW)

summary: This unit teaches you to weld mild steel safely with manual metal arc welding (MMAW), often called stick welding. You will learn to check and set up the machine, choose and care for electrodes, strike and hold an arc, run stringer and weave beads, and make fillet welds on lap and tee joints. You will also learn to clean and inspect your welds, put faults right, finish safely and report problems.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It teaches the basic skills of **manual metal arc welding (MMAW)**: working safely, setting up the machine, choosing and caring for electrodes, striking and holding an arc, running beads, making simple fillet welds, and cleaning, checking and reporting on your work.

MMAW is also called **stick welding** or shielded metal arc welding (SMAW). It is one of the most widely used welding processes in Jamaican workshops and on site: gates, burglar bars, grills, water-tank stands, trailers, farm equipment and building steelwork are all made or repaired with it. The equipment is simple, it works outdoors and it welds most steels, so every welder must master it.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres, and anyone starting out in arc welding of mild steel. You will work on mild steel plate, mostly with E6013 electrodes, with the work laid on the bench.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Spot the hazards of arc welding (electric shock, arc light, fumes, fire, burns) and control them; wear the right PPE; protect the people around you.
Check the machine, leads, electrode holder and work clamp; connect them correctly; set AC or the right DC polarity.
Pick the electrode type and size for the job, set the current from the packet, and keep electrodes dry.
Read the job sheet, cut and clean the metal, fit up and tack the joint, and control distortion.
Strike by scratching or tapping, hold a short, steady arc, and keep the right angle and travel speed.
Run straight (stringer) and weave beads, and make single-run fillet welds on lap and tee joints.
Remove slag, check the weld by eye and with a gauge, name any faults and say how to prevent them.
Shut down, store the equipment and electrodes, leave the bay clean, and report faults, damage and incidents.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on safety, equipment, electrodes, technique, joints, weld faults and clean-up.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact trade terms) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks**: running straight and weave beads on mild steel plate, and fillet welds on lap and tee joints. The assessor watches how you work (safe set-up, PPE, testing the current, cleaning up), not only the finished weld.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms in the Revision section. Short-answer questions ask for exact trade words such as stub, undercut, toe, stringer bead, weld pool and work lead.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Arc welding has five main hazards: **electric shock**, **arc radiation** (the light from the arc), **fumes**, **fire** and **burns**. Chipping and grinding add flying particles and noise. Before every job, look around and ask: what could hurt me or someone else here, and what will I do about it?

head: Hazard
What can happen
How you control it
rows: The electrode, the holder jaws and the work are live whenever the machine is on. If your body completes the circuit, current flows through you. A shock can burn you, stop your heart, or make you fall from a height.
Keep gloves, clothing and boots dry
Never stand in water or weld in the rain
Check the cables, plug, holder and clamp before use
Stand on a dry board or rubber mat on wet or steel floors
Never touch the electrode or holder jaws with bare skin or wet gloves
Switch off before changing anything on the machine

The arc gives off **ultraviolet (UV)** and **infrared (IR)** rays and very bright light. UV burns the eyes (arc eye) and bare skin, like severe sunburn, within seconds to minutes. Light reflected off shiny or pale surfaces burns too.
Helmet with the right filter shade
Screens or curtains round the bay

The flux and the metal give off tiny metal particles and gases. They cause coughing, sore throat and lung damage and, over years, serious illness, including cancer. Paint, oil, plastic and zinc coatings make worse fumes.
Ventilation or extraction close to the arc
Head kept out of the fume plume
Coatings removed from the weld area

Sparks and spatter can fly 10 metres or more and lodge in cracks, wood, rags or rubbish, where they can smoulder for a long time before flaring up. Gas cylinders, fuel and containers that held fuel can explode.
Anything that burns removed or covered
No welding on drums or tanks that held fuel unless a competent person has made them safe
Fire watch during and after the work
Hot plate, slag, spatter and stubs burn. Once steel stops glowing, hot steel looks exactly like cold steel.
Hot work marked HOT with soapstone
Chipping and grinding throw hot, sharp pieces at the eyes. Grinding and hammering are loud enough to damage hearing over time.
Clear safety glasses at all times
Face shield over the glasses when grinding

blocks.p: Dry skin resists electric current; wet skin lets it through easily. In Jamaica's hot, humid weather your gloves and shirt can be soaked with sweat within minutes, and site work often means rain, puddles, wet grass, or kneeling on steel. These are exactly the conditions in which welders get shocked.

ul: Keep a spare pair of dry gloves and change as soon as yours are damp.
Stand or kneel on a dry wooden board or rubber mat, never in water or on wet ground.
Do not weld in the rain. Keep the machine dry, off wet ground and out of puddles.
Take extra care when you sit, lie or kneel on steel, or work in a tight space: your body is then touching the work.
Never drape the leads over your shoulders or wrap them round your body, and never hold the holder under your arm.
Where a machine has a voltage-reducing device (VRD), use it, especially in wet or cramped places.
Drink water and take short breaks out of the heat: a tired, overheated welder makes mistakes.

blocks.note: The voltage that shocks welders is usually the **open-circuit voltage**, which is there whenever the machine is on, even when you are not welding. Turning the current down does not make the holder safe to touch. Dry PPE, sound insulation and switching off do.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: If someone gets an electric shock

flow: Do not touch the person while they may still be in contact with the live lead or holder
Switch off the welding machine, or the power at the mains, at once
If you cannot switch off, push the lead or the person clear with something dry that does not conduct, such as a wooden broom handle
Shout for help and call the emergency services (in Jamaica, dial 110 for fire and ambulance)
If you are trained, check breathing and give CPR if needed; anyone who has had a shock should see a doctor or nurse
Report it to your instructor or supervisor; the machine stays out of use until it has been checked

ul: Before you strike an arc, look about 10 metres around you, including above and below: sparks fall through gaps in floors, walls and ceilings.
Remove anything that can burn: rags, paper, cardboard, wood shavings, dry grass, fuel and paint tins. If something cannot be moved, cover it with a fire-resistant welding blanket.
Keep gas cylinders, fuel cans and vehicles well away from sparks and heat. A cylinder with its valve closed can still leak or burst if it is heated.
Never weld or cut a drum, tank or pipe that has held fuel, oil or chemicals until a competent person has cleaned it and said it is safe. Vapour left inside can explode.
Keep a suitable fire extinguisher (for example dry powder or carbon dioxide) within reach, and know how to use it.
On sites, follow the hot-work permit if the workplace uses one.
Keep a **fire watch** while you weld and after you finish: check for smoke, a burning smell or smouldering for at least 30 minutes, or longer if the workplace's rules say so (many ask for an hour).

blocks.note: Many jobs here are done in yards and homes: grills, gates, burglar bars, tank stands. Look out for the house's cooking-gas cylinder, curtains and wooden window frames, gaps in zinc fences, and dry grass and bush in dry weather. Move what you can, cover what you cannot, and check again before you leave.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Work where air moves through the bay, or use the extraction hood, placed close to the arc.
Keep your head out of the fume plume that rises from the arc. Stand so that moving air carries the fumes away from your face.
Clean off paint, oil, grease and plastic coatings before welding.

**Galvanised** (zinc-coated) steel gives off zinc fume that causes **metal fume fever**: chills, fever, aches and sickness, like flu, a few hours later. Grind the coating off the weld area, use extraction, and wear the respirator your instructor gives you.
Never use chlorinated degreasing solvents near the arc: arc light can turn their vapour into a poisonous gas (phosgene).
If you feel dizzy, sick or short of breath, stop, get into fresh air and tell your instructor.
Weld inside a screened bay, or put up welding screens or curtains on site.
Before you strike, call a warning (for example "Cover!") so people nearby look away or lower their helmets.
Keep visitors, customers and children well away from the work. Sunglasses and clear glasses do **not** protect eyes from arc rays.
Never leave hot metal unmarked, or live leads and cables lying across a walkway.

blocks.p: **PPE** (personal protective equipment) is your last line of defence when a hazard cannot be removed. Wear the full set every time you weld, even for one short tack, and check it before you start.

head: PPE
What it protects you from
What to check
rows: Arc rays, spatter and heat on the eyes, face and neck
Filter shade right for the current
Filter not cracked; clear cover lens not pitted with spatter
Headband fits and the helmet stays down
Auto-darkening helmets: battery, sensors and shade setting work
Flying slag and grinding chips; worn under the helmet
Lenses clean and not badly scratched
Sparks and chips on the face when grinding or chipping
Worn over safety glasses, not instead of them
Heat, spatter, arc rays and electric shock on the hands and wrists
Arc rays and sparks on the skin
Long sleeves rolled down; collar buttoned
No frayed edges, open pockets or turn-ups to catch sparks
Heavier spatter, especially when welding vertical or overhead
Falling steel, hot slag, and shock through the feet
Leather, with toe caps and good soles
Trouser legs worn over the boots, not tucked in
Noise from grinding and chipping; plugs also stop sparks going into the ears
Sparks on the head and hair
Fumes where ventilation or extraction is not enough
The type your instructor or the risk assessment names

blocks.p: The filter shade is a number: the **higher the number, the darker** the lens. More current makes a brighter arc, so it needs a darker shade. Most MMAW work needs a shade between about 10 and 13.

blocks.note: These are guide figures from standard shade charts: follow the chart for your helmet and your instructor. If you cannot see the weld pool clearly, the shade may be too dark; if your eyes ache or you see spots afterwards, it is too light. Shades 3 to 6 are for gas work and do not protect you from an electric arc.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Jamaica's heat tempts welders to roll up their sleeves, or to weld in a vest or a polyester sports shirt. Do not. Arc rays burn bare skin in minutes. **Nylon, polyester and other synthetic fabrics melt** when a spark lands on them and stick to the skin, making a burn much worse. Wear long-sleeved cotton or wool (flame-resistant cotton is best), drink water often, and take short breaks out of the heat.

ul: Take lighters and matches out of your pockets before you weld. A spark or hot spatter can set off a lighter, which can burst.
Keep your clothes free of oil and grease: they catch fire easily.
Button your cuffs and collar and keep pockets closed, so sparks cannot get in.

blocks.note: **Arc eye** (also called welder's flash) is a burn to the surface of the eye from UV rays. It feels like sand in the eyes, with pain, watering and a dislike of light, and it often starts several hours after the exposure, sometimes in the night. Do not rub your eyes. Tell your instructor and see a doctor or nurse. People standing nearby can get arc eye too.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: In MMAW an electric arc burns between a flux-coated electrode and the work. The arc is extremely hot (several thousand degrees Celsius), enough to melt the tip of the electrode and the surface of the plate into a **weld pool**. Drops of metal from the electrode's core wire cross the arc and become part of the weld. The flux coating burns to make a gas shield around the arc and a layer of **slag** over the hot weld, so the air cannot spoil it. As you move along, the pool behind the arc cools and freezes into a **bead**.

flow: Mains supply (110 V or 220 V, 50 Hz) through the plug, cable and switch
Welding machine (power source): changes mains power into a high current at a low voltage
Electrode lead: carries the current to the electrode holder
Electrode: the arc jumps from its tip to the work
Work: the job being welded
Work return clamp and lead: carry the current back to the machine

head: Part
Its job
Check before use
rows: Takes power from the mains and gives a **high current at a low voltage**, AC or DC. You set the current (in amps) on its controls.
Carries the current from the machine to the electrode holder
No cuts, burns or bare copper
Grips the electrode and passes the current to it; its insulated handle protects your hand
Insulation not cracked, burnt or missing
Carries the current from the work back to the machine, completing the circuit
Clamp spring firm and jaws clean
Fixed to clean metal on the job, close to the weld
Let the current pass without heating up
Clean and tight at the machine, holder and clamp
A loose joint gets hot and makes the arc unsteady

blocks.note: The work return lead is often called the earth lead or ground lead, but it is **not** a safety earth: the machine's safety earth comes through its mains plug. Fix the clamp to clean metal on the job, close to the weld. Never use water pipes, gas pipes or the steel of a building as part of the welding circuit.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When the machine is on but you are not welding, the voltage between the electrode and the work is the **open-circuit voltage (OCV)**, often about 50–90 V. It has to be high enough to start the arc. Once the arc is burning, the voltage drops to the **arc voltage**, about 20–30 V, while the current rises to the value you set. Because the OCV is there whenever the machine is on, treat the holder as live at all times.
MMAW machines are **constant-current** machines: the current changes only a little when your arc length changes a little. That is what lets you hold a steady arc by hand.

head: Point
AC (alternating current)
DC (direct current)
rows: Rectifier or inverter (or an engine-driven generator on site); inverters are small and light
Changes direction 100 times a second on Jamaica's 50 Hz supply
Less steady; some electrodes are harder to strike
Smooth and steady; easier to strike and hold
Only those made for AC, such as E6013 and E7018
All common electrodes, at the polarity on the packet
Can happen: magnetism pushes the arc to one side
General mild steel work where a transformer is all you have
Thin metal, vertical and overhead work, low-hydrogen electrodes, most modern work

blocks.p: With DC, the electrode lead can go to the positive (+) or the negative (−) terminal. That choice is the **polarity**. On many machines you change it by swapping the leads between the two sockets; on others there is a switch.

head: Polarity
How it is connected
Typical effect
rows: Electrode lead to +, work return lead to −
Deeper penetration; used for E7018 and most other electrodes on DC
Electrode lead to −, work return lead to +
Electrode melts faster, with shallower penetration; some rutile electrodes run well like this on thin metal

blocks.note: The **electrode maker** decides the polarity: read the packet. "AC/DC+" means AC, or DC with the electrode positive. E6013 usually runs on AC or on either DC polarity. American books call DCEP "reverse polarity" and DCEN "straight polarity".
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The **duty cycle** is how many minutes in every 10 a machine can weld at a given current without overheating. It is printed on the rating plate as a percentage. The lower the current, the higher the duty cycle.

head: Rating plate shows
What it means
rows: At 180 A it can weld for 3½ minutes in every 10, then must rest for 6½ minutes
At 130 A it can weld for 6 minutes in every 10, then must rest for 4 minutes
At 100 A or less it can weld without stopping

blocks.p: Duty cycles are measured at a set air temperature (often 40 °C). In a hot Jamaican workshop, with the machine in the sun or its vents blocked, it will overheat sooner. Most machines have a thermal cut-out that stops the arc and lights a warning lamp when they get too hot.

blocks.note: If the overheat light comes on, stop welding but **leave the machine switched on**: its fan keeps cooling it. Carry on when the light goes out, and from then on weld in shorter spells or at a lower current.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Jamaica's mains supply is 110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz. Read the machine's rating plate and connect it only to the supply it is made for.
Many welding machines need a 220 V outlet on a circuit that can carry their input current. A thin or very long extension lead overheats and makes the machine weld poorly.
Only a qualified electrician installs or repairs mains wiring, plugs and sockets.
Unroll the leads fully. Keep them untangled and out of walkways, where people trip on them and trolleys run over them.
Keep them away from hot metal, sharp edges, oil and water.
Use leads thick enough for the current and no longer than you need: long, thin leads get hot and weaken the arc.
Never lift or drag the machine by its leads.

blocks.p: On DC, magnetism in the job can push the arc to one side, mostly near the ends of a joint or in corners. The arc wanders and spatters and can leave porosity. To control it: move the work clamp, angle the electrode against the blow, weld towards a heavy tack or a finished weld, hold a shorter arc, or change to AC.
An MMAW electrode is a metal rod, the **core wire**, covered with a **flux coating**. One end is bare so the holder can grip it. Most electrodes are 300–450 mm long.

head: Part
Its job
rows: Carries the current, melts in the arc and becomes filler metal in the weld
Burns to make a **gas shield** that keeps air away from the arc and the weld pool
Forms **slag** that covers and protects the hot weld and slows its cooling
Helps the arc to start and stay steady
Cleans the weld metal, and can add alloys or iron powder
Gripped by the holder; takes the current into the core wire
The short end left after use; it goes in a metal stub bin

blocks.note: Stop when about 40–50 mm of electrode is left. Burning it shorter overheats the holder and can burn its jaws.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Mild steel electrodes are often marked with the American (AWS) code, for example E6013 or E7018. Many packets also carry an ISO code; your instructor will show you how to read it.

head: Part of the code
What it tells you
In E6013
In E7018
rows: Minimum tensile strength of the weld metal, in thousands of psi (pounds per square inch)
Welding positions: 1 = all positions; 2 = flat and horizontal fillet only
Type of flux coating and the current it runs on
18 = low-hydrogen coating with iron powder; AC or DC+

head: Electrode
Coating
Current
Used for
Points to know
rows: AC or DC (check the packet for the polarity)
General mild steel work: gates, grills, frames, light fabrication; learning to weld
Smooth, neat bead; slag lifts off easily
Stronger, crack-resistant welds: structural steel, thicker plate, parts that carry load
Must be kept very dry, in a rod oven
Harder for a beginner to strike and restart
E6011: AC or DC+. E6010: DC+ only
Deep penetration: root runs and pipe work
More spatter and a rougher bead

blocks.note: In this unit you will mostly use **E6013**: the usual first choice for a beginner on mild steel, on AC or DC.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Choosing the size and the current

blocks.p: An electrode's size is the diameter of its **core wire**, not of the coating. Thicker metal needs a bigger electrode and more current.

head: Electrode size
Typical use
Typical current for E6013
rows: Sheet and light sections, about 1.5–3 mm
Thicker plate, about 8 mm and up
Heavy plate, mostly in the flat position

blocks.note: These are typical figures only. Every maker prints a current range on the packet: **use that range, start near the middle and test on scrap**. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and your instructor.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When you change one thing, check the current again:

ul: **Electrode size:** a smaller electrode needs less current; a larger one needs more.
**Plate thickness:** thicker plate needs more heat, because heat flows away from the weld faster.
**Fillet welds:** usually a little more current than a bead on plate of the same thickness, because the heat flows into two plates.
**Vertical and overhead welding:** usually less current, so the pool does not run.
**AC or DC:** the packet may give a different range for each.

blocks.p: The flux coating soaks up moisture from the air. **Damp flux** causes porosity, a spattery, unsteady arc and, with low-hydrogen electrodes, cracking. Jamaica's humid air makes this a daily problem, especially in the rainy seasons.

ul: Keep electrodes in their sealed packet or in a closed, dry cabinet, off the floor and away from doors, windows and water.
Take out only what you will use soon, and put unused electrodes back.

Once a box of low-hydrogen electrodes (E7018) is opened, keep them in a heated holding oven (often about 120–150 °C). If they have picked up moisture, re-bake them at the temperature and for the time on the packet (often about 350 °C for 1 to 2 hours). Never guess.
Some E7018 come in sealed vacuum packs that can be used straight from the pack. Once a pack is opened, use the electrodes within the time the maker gives.
If E6013 gets damp, it can usually be dried at a much lower temperature, as the packet says. Do not bake it at E7018 temperatures: that can spoil the coating.
Hand in to your instructor any electrode with cracked, chipped or crumbling flux, or with a rusty bare end.

blocks.p: Before you weld, read the drawing or job sheet. It tells you the metal and its thickness, the joint, the type and size of weld, and the welding position.

head: Joint
How the parts meet
Usual weld
rows: Edge to edge, in the same flat line
Butt weld, filling the gap or groove between the edges
One plate stands on the face of the other, making a T
Fillet weld in one or both corners
Two plates overlap, one lying on top of the other
Fillet weld along the edge of the top plate, often on both edges
Two plate edges meet at an angle, usually 90°, making an L
Fillet weld inside, or a weld along the outside corner
Two plates lie face to face with their edges level
A run along the edges; used mainly on thin sheet

blocks.p: A **fillet weld** has a roughly triangular section and joins two surfaces at about a right angle, as in tee, lap and inside corner joints. A **butt weld** joins parts edge to edge.
Thin plate can be butt welded with square edges and a small gap. Thicker plate needs its edges bevelled so the arc can reach the bottom of the joint, the **root**.

head: Preparation
Typical use
Typical sizes (always follow the drawing)
rows: Thin plate, up to about 3 mm, welded from one side
Plate from about 6 mm, welded from one side
Included angle about 60° (30° on each plate)
Thick plate, welded from both sides
Needs less weld metal than a single-V and pulls the plate less out of line

flow: Mark out with a steel rule, a square, and soapstone or a scriber
Cut to size (guillotine, hacksaw, abrasive cut-off saw, or gas or plasma cutting) and remove the burrs
Bevel the edges if the drawing asks for it, by grinding or filing, leaving the root face
Clean the weld area to bright metal, about 25 mm each side of the joint: wire-brush or grind off rust, mill scale and paint, and wipe off oil and grease
Fit up the parts and check the alignment, gap and squareness with an engineer's square and a rule

blocks.p: **Mill scale** is the blue-black skin on hot-rolled steel. Rust, scale, paint and oil spoil a weld: they cause porosity, slag inclusions and poor fusion.

blocks.note: When grinding: wear safety glasses and a face shield; check that the disc is the right type, rated for the grinder's speed and not cracked; keep the guard on; hold the grinder with both hands; and unplug it before changing the disc. Point the sparks away from people and from anything that can burn.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Tack welds** are short welds that hold the parts in place and in line while you make the full weld.

ul: Put a tack at each end of a short joint, and more at even spacing along a long one.
Keep tacks short (often about 10–15 mm) and small, but well fused, so the full weld can melt them in.
Lap joint: clamp the plates flat and tight together, tack each end, and check there is no gap between the plates.
Tee joint: tack each end, then check the upright plate with an engineer's square; while the tacks are still small, it can be tapped square.
Chip the slag off the tacks before you weld over them.
Frame: tack every joint and check the frame (square, and the diagonals equal) before you fully weld any joint.

blocks.p: Heat makes steel expand. As the weld and the metal beside it cool, they **shrink** and pull on the parts. This bends, twists or pulls the job out of line: **distortion**. The more heat and weld metal you put in, the more distortion you get.

head: Method
How it helps
rows: Holds the parts in position and in line before the full weld
Holds the parts firmly while the weld cools
Sets the parts slightly out of line, the opposite way to the pull, so the shrinking weld pulls them straight
Welds opposite sides or corners in turn, so the pulls cancel each other out
Welds short lengths in a planned order, so the heat is spread out
The right size of weld and current
Extra weld metal and extra heat mean extra shrinking, so do not over-weld

blocks.note: Throwing water on a weld does not stop it shrinking, and fast cooling can crack some steels. Let welds cool in air unless your instructor says otherwise.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Striking the arc and running welds

flow: Area: screens up, anything that burns cleared away, extinguisher ready, ventilation on, floor dry
You: full PPE on, gloves dry, lighters out of your pockets
Equipment: mains cable, leads, holder and clamp undamaged; connections tight
Job: cleaned, fitted and tacked; work clamp on clean metal near the weld
Electrode: right type and size, dry, with its coating whole
Settings: AC, or the DC polarity on the packet; current near the middle of the packet's range
Test: run a short bead on scrap of the same thickness, and adjust
Warn the people nearby, lower your helmet, strike

blocks.p: Set the current near the middle of the range on the packet. Run a short bead on scrap plate of the same thickness, chip off the slag and look at it. Adjust in small steps (about 5–10 A) until the arc is steady and the bead is even.

head: What you see and hear
Likely cause
What to do
rows: The electrode sticks and the arc keeps going out
The bead is tall and narrow and sits on top of the plate
Turn the current up a little
Lots of spatter; the electrode glows red
The bead is wide and flat, with grooves (undercut) at the edges
Turn the current down a little
A steady crackle, like bacon frying
An even bead with fine, even ripples that blends smoothly into the plate
Keep the setting, and check it again on the job

head: Method
How to do it
Notes
rows: Drag the tip across the plate like striking a match, then lift it at once to the right arc length
Easiest for beginners, and on AC
Bring the tip straight down to touch the plate lightly, then lift it at once to the right arc length
Cleaner; good in tight places and on DC; takes practice

ul: Strike **in the joint**, on the line the weld will cover, for example just ahead of where the bead starts. Never strike on the plate beside the joint, on the bench or on the clamp: stray **arc strikes** leave hard spots and small cracks.

If the electrode **sticks**, keep your helmet down and twist or snap it free with a quick sideways movement. If it will not come free, open the holder to release it, or switch off. A stuck electrode quickly gets red-hot, and it can re-arc as it breaks free.
A used electrode has a small cup of flux at its tip that can stop it striking. Scratch firmly to break the cup.

blocks.p: Many welders remember the five settings as **CLAMS**: Current, Length of arc, Angle, Manipulation and Speed. Get all five right and the bead looks after itself.

head: Setting
About right (typical)
Signs it is wrong
rows: Within the packet's range, adjusted by testing on scrap
Too high: spatter, red-hot electrode, wide flat bead, undercut, burn-through
Too low: sticking, arc going out, tall narrow bead, poor fusion, trapped slag
About the core wire diameter (about 3 mm for a 3.2 mm electrode), and a little shorter for E7018. Feed the electrode down steadily as it burns away.
Too long: hissing and popping, spatter, wide flat bead, porosity, undercut
Too short: the electrode sticks or pushes into the pool; tall, narrow bead
Bead on plate: 70–80° to the plate, with the top of the electrode leaning the way you are travelling, so the tip points back at the weld. Seen from the end: square (90°) to the plate.
Too upright, or leaning backwards: slag runs ahead of the pool and gets trapped
Leaning over too far: the arc is hard to control; poor fusion; uneven bead
Stringer bead: straight along the line, no side movement. Weave bead: a steady side-to-side pattern, pausing briefly at each edge.
Weave too wide, or no pause at the edges: undercut, trapped slag, poor fusion at the sides
Jerky movement: uneven width and ripples
Steady, so the bead stays the same width (a stringer is about 2–3 times the core wire diameter wide), with even, slightly curved ripples
Too fast: thin, narrow bead with long, pointed ripples; poor fusion; undercut
Too slow: wide, heavy bead that rolls over the edges (overlap); slag runs ahead of the pool; too much heat

blocks.note: To tell a current fault from a speed fault, watch the arc and the electrode, not only the bead. Wrong current changes how the arc behaves and how hot the electrode gets. Wrong speed mainly changes the width of the bead and the shape of its ripples.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Mark straight, evenly spaced lines on the clean plate with soapstone
Get comfortable: brace your arm or hand so you can move smoothly along the whole line, and make sure you can see it
Strike at the start of the line (or just ahead of it, then move back) and let the pool form
Hold the arc length and the angle; feed the electrode down as it burns
Travel at a steady speed, watching the edges of the pool and keeping the slag behind it
At the end, pause briefly to fill the crater, then lift away
Chip and brush off the slag, check the bead, and let the plate cool

blocks.p: A **weave bead** is made by moving the electrode from side to side as you travel. It makes a wider bead, to fill a wider joint or to cap a bevelled butt joint.

ul: Common patterns are zigzag, crescent (half-moon) and figure-of-eight. Use the one your instructor shows you.
Keep the weave no wider than about 2½ to 3 times the core wire diameter.
Pause briefly at each edge so the metal fills the toe: this stops undercut.
Cross the middle a little faster so the centre does not build up too high.
Move forward by the same amount each time so the ripples are even.
Never snap the electrode away at the end of a bead. That leaves a **crater**, a hollow that can crack. Pause to fill the crater, or move back a short way over the bead, then lift away.

When an electrode runs out part-way: chip the slag off the crater, fit a new electrode, strike about 10–15 mm ahead of the crater on the weld line, bring the arc back to fill the crater, then carry on forward.

blocks.h: Fillet welds on lap and tee joints

blocks.p: A fillet weld must melt into **both plates** and into the **root** (the inside corner). Clean both plates, tack them, and set the current a little higher than for a bead on plate of the same thickness.

head: Point
Lap joint
Tee joint
rows: Overlap the plates (often about 25 mm, or as drawn), clamp them flat and tight together, tack each end
Stand the upright plate on the base plate, tack each end, check it square
Electrode angle seen from the end
About 45° into the corner, with the arc aimed a little more at the bottom plate so the thin top edge does not melt away
About 45°, halfway between the two plates
70–80° to the joint (a lean of 10–20°) in the direction of travel
70–80° to the joint (a lean of 10–20°) in the direction of travel
Top edge melted off; weld not fused into the bottom plate
Undercut on the upright plate; weld metal sagging and lying unfused on the base plate (overlap)

blocks.note: A tee or lap joint laid on the bench is welded as a **horizontal fillet** (position PB, also called 2F). Gravity pulls the pool down onto the lower plate, so keep a short arc, do not weave wide, and watch the upper toe for undercut.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Let the weld cool for a moment, until the slag has gone dark.
Chip with a **chipping hammer**, striking away from your face and from other people, then clean the bead and its toes with a **wire brush**.
Wear clear safety glasses under your helmet, so your eyes are covered when you lift the helmet to chip: hot slag chips fly.
On a weld of several runs, remove every bit of slag before the next run, or it will be trapped in the weld.
Use a power wire brush or a grinder only with safety glasses, a face shield and the guard in place.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The outer surface of the weld
The line where the face of the weld meets the parent metal
The deepest part of the joint, which the weld must reach
On a fillet weld, the distance from the root to the toe on each plate
On a fillet weld, the distance from the root to the face, through the middle; on an even, flat-faced fillet it is about 0.7 × the leg length
How deep the weld has melted into the parent metal, or through the joint
Weld metal standing above the plate surface on a butt weld
The parent metal beside the weld that was heated enough to change, but did not melt

blocks.p: At this level you inspect welds **by eye** (visual inspection) and with simple gauges, after the slag is off. Look along the weld from both ends and from the side.

head: Check
A good weld
rows: Straight, even in width and height, with fine, even ripples
Blend smoothly into the plate: no groove (undercut) and no metal lying on the surface (overlap)
No holes, cracks or trapped slag; little spatter
Start fully fused; crater filled; no stray arc strikes on the plate
Leg length as the drawing says (checked with a fillet gauge); legs equal; face flat or slightly convex; fused into both plates
Parts still square and in line; sizes as the drawing says

blocks.p: A **fillet gauge** is held against the plates and the weld to check the leg length (and, on some gauges, the throat). Your instructor may also cut through or break a test piece to show how far the weld has fused inside.

head: Fault
What it looks like
Main causes
How to prevent it
rows: Small round gas holes, on the surface or hidden inside
Rust, paint, oil, scale or zinc on the plate
Wind or arc blow disturbing the gas shield
Shelter the arc; control arc blow
A groove melted into the plate along the toe and left unfilled
Travel too fast; no pause at the edges of a weave
Steady speed; pause at the edges
Weld metal spilled over the plate at the toe, lying on it but not fused to it
Wrong angle, letting the pool sag onto the lower plate
Slag trapped in the weld or between runs
Slag not cleaned off between runs
Slag running ahead of the pool (wrong angle or too slow)
Keep the pool ahead of the slag
Weld metal not melted into the plate or into the run below
Aim the arc at both sides of the joint
The weld has not reached right through the root of the joint
Gap too small or root face too big
Electrode too big for the root
Smaller electrode for the root run
Holes melted through the plate, or weld metal hanging below it
Travel too slow on thin metal
Lines in or beside the weld; crater cracks are often star-shaped
Fast cooling of thick or hard steel
Weld too small for the load
Small balls of metal stuck to the plate around the weld
Small burnt spots on the plate away from the weld
Hang the holder up; never lay it on the job
Width and ripples vary; the bead wanders off the line
Brace your arm and get comfortable

blocks.note: **Cracks** are the most serious fault: they can grow and make the job fail. Always show a crack to your instructor. It is usually ground out completely and re-welded.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: When you find a fault, name it, give its likely cause, and say what you will change on the next bead. That is what the assessor wants to hear when you check another trainee's work.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Finish the run and fill the crater
Take the stub out of the holder and drop it in the metal stub bin
Hang the holder on its insulated hook, where it cannot touch the job, the bench or the floor
Switch off at the machine, then at the mains
Coil the leads loosely and hang them up off the floor
Put unused electrodes back in their packet or in the rod oven
Leave hot work to cool in a safe place, marked HOT; move it with tongs
Sweep up slag, stubs and spatter, and check the area for anything smouldering
Return tools and PPE, and report any faults

ul: Keep the bay clear: no offcuts, stubs or tools on the floor, and leads out of walkways.
Stubs stay hot and roll underfoot. Put them in a **metal** container, never a paper or plastic bin.
Keep the floor dry and free of oil.
Keep extinguishers, fire exits and the main switch clear and easy to reach.
Store gas cylinders for cutting upright and chained, away from the welding bays.

blocks.p: Tell your instructor or supervisor **straight away** about anything in the table below. Reporting is not getting someone into trouble: it is how faults are put right before someone is hurt.

head: What to report
Examples
What to do
rows: Cut or burnt cable, cracked holder, weak clamp, damaged plug, a machine that trips or smells of burning
Stop using it, switch off and unplug it, tag it DO NOT USE, and report it. Do not repair mains equipment yourself.
Burns, arc eye, an electric shock, cuts, something in the eye
Get first aid, tell your instructor, and make sure it is written in the accident book
A tingle from the holder, a small fire put out, a spark that landed near a gas cylinder
Report it so the cause is found and fixed before someone is hurt
An extinguisher used even briefly, an empty first-aid box, a torn screen
Report it so it is refilled, replaced or repaired
Damp or damaged electrodes, the wrong electrodes in a packet, plate running short
Report it so stock is dried, replaced or reordered
Faults you could not correct, the job finished, measurements taken
Tell your instructor or supervisor, and fill in the job card or logbook

blocks.note: Training centres and workplaces keep a record of accidents and near misses, and your instructor or supervisor will know what must be reported further. Your part is simple: report at once, say exactly what happened, and help to put it right.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can name the hazards of MMAW (shock, arc radiation, fumes, fire, burns) and say how to control each one.
I can explain why sweat, rain and wet ground raise the risk of electric shock, and what to do about it.
I can say what to do first when someone gets an electric shock.
I can choose and check my PPE, including a filter shade to suit the current.
I can make the work area safe from fire, keep a fire watch, and protect other people from arc light.
I can name the parts of the welding circuit and say what each one does.
I can explain AC and DC, DC polarity, open-circuit voltage and duty cycle.
I can read an electrode code such as E6013 or E7018 and choose an electrode type and size for a job.
I can set the current from the packet, test it on scrap, and adjust it from what the bead shows.
I can store electrodes so that they stay dry.
I can name the five basic joints, and prepare, fit and tack a joint.
I can explain why distortion happens and how to control it.
I can strike an arc by scratching and by tapping, in the joint, and free a stuck electrode safely.
I can hold the right arc length, electrode angle and travel speed.
I can run stringer and weave beads, fill the crater, and restart a bead neatly.
I can make single-run fillet welds on lap and tee joints.
I can remove slag safely and inspect a weld by eye and with a fillet gauge.
I can name the common weld faults, with their causes and how to prevent them.
I can shut down, clean up, and store the equipment and electrodes safely.
I can report faults, damage, injuries and near misses.

terms: Alternating current (changes direction many times a second) and direct current (flows one way only)
The unit in which welding current is measured
The arc being pushed to one side by magnetism, mainly on DC
A painful burn to the surface of the eye from the arc's UV rays; also called welder's flash
The gap between the electrode tip and the weld pool; about the core wire diameter
A single run of weld metal
Two parts meeting edge to edge in the same flat line
The metal rod in the middle of an electrode; it becomes filler metal
The hollow left at the end of a bead if it is not filled
Bending or pulling out of line, caused by the weld shrinking as it cools
How many minutes in every 10 a machine can weld at a given current
The insulated clamp that grips the electrode and carries current to it
A roughly triangular weld joining two surfaces at about a right angle
The coating on the electrode; it makes the gas shield and the slag
Two plates overlapping, one lying on top of the other
Manual metal arc welding; also called stick welding or SMAW
The voltage between electrode and work when the machine is on but not welding
Weld metal lying on the plate at the toe without being fused to it
How deep the weld melts into the parent metal
Which DC terminal (+ or −) the electrode lead is connected to
Gas holes trapped in the weld metal
The glassy crust, formed from the flux, that covers and protects the hot weld
Small balls of metal thrown out by the arc that stick to the plate around the weld
A straight bead made with no side-to-side movement
The short end of an electrode left in the holder after use
A short weld that holds parts in place before the full weld is made
One plate standing on the face of another, making a T
The line where the face of the weld meets the plate
A groove melted into the plate along the toe and left unfilled
A wider bead made by moving the electrode from side to side
The pool of melted metal under the arc
The lead and clamp that carry the current from the work back to the machine; also called the earth or ground lead

c1.title: Burglar bars on a verandah in Portmore
c1.text: Kemar, a Level 2 trainee on work experience, is helping a small fabrication business weld new burglar bars to a steel frame on a verandah in Portmore, St Catherine. It rained in the morning and there are puddles on the tiled floor. It is 33 °C, and Kemar's leather gloves and cotton shirt are soaked with sweat. The 220 V welding machine is plugged in inside the house. The family's cooking-gas cylinder stands by the kitchen door about 3 metres from the work, there are curtains just inside the window, and two children from next door have come to watch.

c2.title: A day of gate work in May Pen
c2.text: Tashana has just started at a small shop in May Pen, Clarendon, that makes steel gates. She is welding 6 mm flat bar into gate frames with 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes; the packet gives 90–130 A, and she has set 120 A. The DC machine's rating plate reads: 200 A at 30%, 140 A at 60%, 110 A at 100%. The shop gets very hot in the afternoon, when the sun shines on the machine through the open side of the building.

c3.title: Pinholes in pump-stand brackets in Montego Bay
c3.text: Andre works in a small steel shop in Montego Bay, St James, welding brackets of 10 mm mild steel plate for a hotel's water-pump stands. The supervisor has asked for E7018 electrodes. It is the rainy season, and the box, opened two weeks ago, has stood on a shelf by the open roller door ever since. The plate has blue-black mill scale and patches of rust. Andre's welds show small pinholes, and he admits he holds a long arc "to see the pool better". The shop's machine is DC, and the packet says "AC or DC+".

c4.title: A water-tank stand in Mandeville
c4.text: At a fabrication shop in Mandeville, Manchester, Dwayne and a trainee, Sasha-Kay, are building a stand of 6 mm mild steel angle and plate for a large plastic water tank. The corners are tee and lap joints, welded with 3.2 mm E6013 electrodes (packet range 90–130 A). On the first corner, Sasha-Kay fully welded one joint before tacking the others, and the frame was pulled out of square. On a tee joint laid on the bench, her current is set at 145 A, and there is a groove melted along the toe on the upright plate. The drawing asks for 6 mm fillet welds.

c5.title: Closing down a welding bay in Spanish Town
c5.text: At the end of an evening class at a training centre in Spanish Town, Ricardo is asked to close down Bay 3. Earlier, another trainee used the bay's fire extinguisher for a few seconds to put out a smouldering rag, then hung it back on its bracket. Ricardo also tells a classmate that he felt a tingle in his hand when he changed an electrode with sweaty gloves, although he was not hurt.

questions.q: Before Kemar strikes the next arc, which change does most to cut his risk of an electric shock?
o: Turn the current down so less electricity can pass through him
Wrap extra insulating tape round the electrode holder's handle
Put on dry gloves and stand on a dry board, clear of the water
Fix the work clamp further away from where he is welding
questions.why: Sweat and rain water let current pass through skin far more easily, so dry gloves and a dry insulating surface keep him out of the circuit. Turning the current down does not remove the open-circuit voltage that gives the shock.

questions.q: What should be done about the cooking-gas cylinder before welding starts?
o: Have it moved well away from the sparks, with an extinguisher ready
Close its valve tightly, since a closed cylinder cannot catch fire or burst
Turn it so that its valve faces away from where he is welding
Leave it and weld in short bursts so that fewer sparks fly
questions.why: Sparks and spatter can fly 10 metres or more, and a heated cylinder can leak or burst even with its valve closed. Move gas cylinders and anything that burns well away, and keep an extinguisher at hand.

questions.q: The two children want to stay and watch. What should Kemar do?
o: Let them watch from 3 metres away as long as they wear sunglasses
Lend them his clear safety glasses so that their eyes are covered
Let them watch from behind him, out of the line of the sparks
Ask an adult to keep them away from the work area while he welds
questions.why: Arc rays burn the eyes of anyone who can see the arc, directly or by reflection, and sunglasses or clear glasses do not filter them. Onlookers, especially children, are kept out of the area, and screens are used where people must pass.

questions.q: Kemar finishes the last bar at 4:00 p.m. What should happen before the team leaves the house?
o: They cool the new bars with water before anyone in the family can touch them
Someone checks inside and out for smouldering for at least 30 minutes
They close all the windows so no stray sparks can blow inside later
They sweep up the slag and leave, as the arc is now switched off
questions.why: A spark can lodge in a curtain, a wooden frame or a crack and smoulder unseen before it flares up. A fire watch during and after hot work catches this; follow the workplace's rule if it asks for longer.

questions.q: Tashana's test bead on scrap is thin and narrow, with long, pointed ripples. The arc crackled steadily and the electrode did not stick or glow. What is the most likely cause?
o: The current was set too low for the electrode
She travelled along the plate too fast
The current was set too high for the electrode
She held the electrode at too steep an angle
questions.why: Wrong current shows in the arc and the electrode: sticking when it is too low, spatter and a glowing electrode when it is too high. A normal arc with a thin bead and pointed ripples means the travel was too fast.

questions.q: Midway through a weld, Tashana's electrode sticks to the frame. What should she do?
o: Lift her helmet to see it clearly, then pull it straight up off the work
Turn the current up while it is stuck so the electrode burns itself free
Let go of the holder and wait for the stuck electrode to cool down
Keep her helmet down and twist it free, or open the holder to release it
questions.why: A stuck electrode carries a short-circuit current, glows red-hot and can re-arc as it breaks free, so the helmet stays down. Twist and snap it free; if that fails, open the holder's jaws or switch the machine off.

questions.q: In the afternoon the machine's overheat light comes on and the arc stops. What should Tashana do?
o: Leave it on so its fan cools it, and wait for the light to go out
Switch it off at the mains at once so that it can cool down faster
Switch it off and on again to reset it, then carry on welding as before
Take off the case cover and blow out the dust, then carry on
questions.why: The thermal cut-out protects the machine, and its fan keeps cooling it only while it is switched on. Afterwards, keep it out of the sun and weld in shorter spells or at a lower current.

questions.q: The gates need long welds. According to the rating plate, what is the highest current at which the machine can weld without stopping to rest?
o: 140 A, the 60% figure on the plate
200 A, the highest figure on the plate
110 A, the 100% figure on the plate
130 A, the top of the packet's range
questions.why: At its 100% current a machine can weld non-stop; at 140 A this one can weld only 6 minutes in every 10. The rating is for a set air temperature, so in a very hot shop it may still cut out sooner.

questions.q: Part-way along a weld, Tashana's electrode burns down to a stub. After fitting a new one, how should she carry on?
o: Strike right in the middle of the old crater and carry straight on from there
Start the new run about 25 mm past the crater and fill the gap at the end
Strike on the plate beside the weld, then drag the arc across into the crater
Chip the crater, strike just ahead of it, come back to fill it, then go on
questions.why: Striking just ahead, on the line the weld will cover, lets the arc settle before it comes back to fill the crater, so the join is fused and smooth. A strike beside the joint leaves an arc strike on the plate.

questions.q: Which things in Andre's story can each cause the pinholes (porosity)?
o: The DC machine, the thick plate and the long arc
Damp electrodes, rusty plate and the long arc
Damp electrodes, the DC machine and the thick plate
The thick plate, the rusty plate and the DC machine
questions.why: Moisture in the flux and rust or scale on the plate give off gas in the arc, and a long arc lets air reach the pool. E7018 runs well on DC+, and 10 mm plate does not cause porosity.

questions.q: Why would the supervisor choose E7018 rather than E6013 for these brackets?
o: It is easier to strike, and its slag peels off much more easily
It can be stored anywhere, as its coating does not take up damp
It gives stronger, crack-resistant welds for load-bearing parts
It is the only type of electrode that will run on a DC machine
questions.why: E7018 is a low-hydrogen electrode with a higher minimum strength (70 000 psi against 60 000 psi), chosen where welds carry load or must resist cracking. It is harder to use than E6013 and must be kept very dry.

questions.q: What should the shop do with the rest of the opened box?
o: Lay them out in the sun for a day to dry, then put them back on the shelf
Use them up quickly on less important jobs, then buy a fresh box
Tape the box shut so no more damp air gets in, and keep using them
Re-bake them as the packet says, then keep them in a holding oven
questions.why: Damp low-hydrogen electrodes put hydrogen into the weld, causing porosity and cracking. Re-bake them at the maker's temperature and time, keep them in a holding oven, and take out only what will be used soon.

questions.q: How should Andre connect the leads for these electrodes on the DC machine?
o: Electrode lead to +, work return lead to −
Electrode lead to −, work return lead to +
Either way round: "DC+" only means DC may be used
He cannot use DC for E7018; he needs an AC machine
questions.why: DC+ (DCEP) means the electrode is positive: the electrode lead goes to the + terminal and the work return lead to −, with the clamp on clean metal on the job. Always use the polarity printed on the packet.

questions.q: What should Sasha-Kay have done to stop the frame being pulled out of square?
o: Welded the first corner faster, at a higher current, to put in less heat
Left out the tacks altogether, since they only get in the way of the full weld
Tacked all the joints and checked the frame square before full welding
Cooled each finished weld with water straight away to stop it shrinking
questions.why: A weld shrinks as it cools and pulls the parts with it. Tacking all the joints first, checking square, clamping, and then welding in a balanced order keep the frame in line.

questions.q: The groove along the toe of Sasha-Kay's tee joint is undercut. What should she change first?
o: Turn the current up so more metal fills the groove
Bring the current down into the packet's range
Hold a longer arc so the heat spreads out wider
Travel faster so the arc spends less time at the toe
questions.why: Undercut comes from too much current, too long an arc, travelling too fast or the wrong angle. Her 145 A is above the packet's 90–130 A, so she brings it down first, then keeps a short arc at about 45° between the plates.

questions.q: How should Dwayne check that the finished fillets meet the drawing's 6 mm size?
o: Chip off the slag, then measure the legs with a fillet gauge
Measure across the face of the hot weld with a steel rule
Compare the weld by eye with the size of the electrode used
Strike the joint with a hammer to see whether the weld holds
questions.why: Fillet size is given as the leg length (some drawings give the throat), and a fillet gauge measures it. Check after the slag is off, so the true shape shows, and check that both legs are equal.

questions.q: What should happen about the fire extinguisher?
o: Leave it: it was used for only a few seconds, so it is still nearly full
Shake it well so the powder settles, then leave it on its bracket
Report its use so it is recharged or replaced before the next class
Move it to the floor by the bay so the next class sees it was used
questions.why: An extinguisher that has been used, even briefly, may lose pressure and fail next time. Every use is reported so it is recharged or replaced, and so the fire is recorded.

questions.q: What should Ricardo do about the tingle he felt?
o: Ignore it, as a small tingle is normal when welding in hot weather
Tell the instructor so it is recorded and the cause is checked
Mention it only if it happens again with a stronger shock
Turn the current down next time so that any tingle is weaker
questions.why: A tingle means current found a path through his body, often through sweat-soaked gloves or damaged insulation. Reporting it as a near miss gets the cause fixed before someone is badly hurt.

questions.q: Kadian is welding with 3.2 mm electrodes at about 120 A. Which filter shade would a standard shade chart suggest for his helmet?
o: Shade 3 or 4
Shade 5 or 6
Shade 13 or 14
Shade 10 or 11
questions.why: Shade charts give about 10–11 for MMAW at around 80–175 A, and darker shades for higher currents. Shades 3 to 6 are for gas work and far too light for an arc, while 13 or 14 would hide the weld pool at this current.

questions.q: A farmer from St Elizabeth brings a galvanised (zinc-coated) gate post to be welded. What should you do first?
o: Grind the zinc off the weld area and set up fume extraction
Weld straight over the zinc, as it helps the weld resist rust
Turn the current up high so the zinc burns off more quickly
Put on a dust mask and weld straight over the coating
questions.why: Burning zinc gives off fume that causes metal fume fever (flu-like chills, fever and sickness), and the coating also causes porosity. Remove it from the weld area and use extraction, with the respirator your instructor gives you.
